ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This research complied with the American Psychological Association Code of Ethics and was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Clemson University.
Participants completed a series of drives in which the automation avoided road hazards successfully, but the system experienced a transient failure midway through the experiment.
To specifically examine the relationship between WM and trust, participants were placed in a situation where the reliability of automation changed abruptly, between blocks.
Participants were informed they were collaborating with automation on a task, and that they should try to maximize their combined score.
Participants completed three experimental blocks with automated memory tasks and manual arithmetic tasks.
At the end of each block, participants were asked to evaluate their level of trust in the memory task aid using the question, "How much did you trust this automated memory aid?"
Due to an experimental error, only 70 of the 111 subjects completed the PAS scale (33 in the low workload and 37 in the high workload).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Individual differences in cognitive abilities may influence how people develop and maintain trust in automated systems, yet the mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood.

This study investigated how three foundational cognitive abilities -working memory (WM), attention control (AC), and fluid intelligence (Gf) -shape trust dynamics, particularly focusing on trust decline and recovery after automation failures.

Participants (n=111) completed cognitive tests measuring WM, AC, and Gf before performing a dual-task paradigm where they monitored an automated memory aid exhibiting varying reliability levels (100%-65%-100%) while completing a mental arithmetic task.

Results revealed that WM and Gf positively predicted trust recovery after automation failures, while AC influenced long-term trust calibration, with high-AC individuals showing more nuanced trust adjustments reflecting system reliability history.
Trust decline was uniform across ability levels, suggesting immediacy of trust loss.
The relationship between abilities and trust may have been partially mediated by automation schemas, with WM negatively correlating with all-or-none thinking about automation.

These findings suggest different cognitive abilities play distinct roles in trust dynamics: WM supports monitoring automation performance, Gf enables effective schema updating, and AC facilitates appropriate deployment of these resources for trust calibration.
This work advances our understanding of trust mechanisms and has implications for designing automation interfaces that accommodate individual cognitive differences.
Automation has expanded from specialized domains to everyday life, including vehicles, entertainment, and shopping.
While reliable automation can reduce workload and improve performance (Wickens & Dixon, 2007), failures can erode user trust (Lee & Moray, 1994; Lee & See, 2004).

text.text: Since trust influences automation use (Muir, 1987), recovering it after failures is crucial for continued use.

text.text: Trust recovery can be active (trust repair) or passive.

While research shows machines can actively repair trust (de Visser et al., 2018; Pak & Rovira, 2023), this may not always be feasible due to practical limitations or because effective trust repair strategies are highly context dependent.

text.text: Thus, understanding passive trust recovery and its influencing factors is crucial.

Research shows trust tends to recover naturally after automation failure, assuming no subsequent errors.

Trust dropped after this failure but recovered once the fault disappeared.
However, the extent of recovery differed across studies.
Whereas Lee and Moray saw trust return to pre-failure levels, Mishler and Chen noted incomplete recovery, suggesting full recovery may require more time.
These studies demonstrate passive trust recovery occurs, but its extent and duration may vary.

These findings support the notion of a cognitive knowledge structure, the schema, that influences users' perceptions of automated systems, and therefore affects trust.

Although the cognitive factors that contribute to the building and updating of automation schemas have not been empirically studied, schema updating is known to depend on cognitive abilities such as working memory (Radvansky & Dijkstra, 2007).

text.text: This could be because lower WM individuals lack resources to maintain information about automation performance and update their schemas, leading to inappropriate trust calibration (i.e., under-or over-trust).
In contrast, those with higher WM may have spare resources to analyze automation performance and calibrate trust appropriately.
Individuals with low working memory (WM) may struggle to remember and integrate past automation failures into their schema, potentially leading to overtrust compared to those with high WM.

text.text: To specifically examine the relationship between WM and trust, participants were placed in a situation where the reliability of automation changed abruptly, between blocks.
We then examined how individual differences in WM related to trust dynamics as reliability changed.
This study also explores how two cognitive abilities closely linked to WM might influence the results: fluid intelligence (Gf) and attention control (AC).
Gf is the capacity to solve novel problems and adapt to new situations (Engle et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Gf is the capacity to solve novel problems and adapt to new situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Engle et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of trust calibration, Gf may help users recognize patterns in automation performance, interpret what changes in reliability mean, and revise their automation schema when new evidence conflicts with prior expectations.
In this way, Gf may support more accurate trust calibration by helping users update their understanding of the automation over time.

AC, which researchers also refer to as cognitive control, executive control (Botvinick et al., 2001), or inhibition (Miyake & Friedman, 2012), is the ability to regulate information processing to achieve goal-directed behavior (Burgoyne & Engle, 2000).
text.formatted: AC, which researchers also refer to as cognitive control, executive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Botvinick et al., 2001)</ref>, or inhibition <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Miyake & Friedman, 2012)</ref>, is the ability to regulate information processing to achieve goal-directed behavior <ref type="bibr">(Burgoyne & Engle, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of trust calibration, AC may help users allocate attention to reliability-relevant automation cues while disengaging from irrelevant information.
This attentional regulation may support a more accurate evaluation of automation performance, which may in turn contribute to a more accurate automation schema and bettercalibrated trust.
WM, Gf, and AC are related but conceptually distinct abilities.
Both Gf and AC have consistently shown strong relationships with WM (Draheim et al., 2022; Pak et al., 2023; Kyllonen & Christal, 1990; Burgoyne & Engle, 2000).

text.text: Recent research has revealed that AC functions as a higher-level executive system that coordinates the deployment of either Gf or WM based on task requirements (Burgoyne et al., 2023).

text.text: Specifically, when a task demands information maintenance over time, AC engages WM processes.
However, when faced with goal conflicts or distractions, AC activates Gf to resolve these conflicts.

Consistent with this view, Draheim et al. (2021) demonstrated that the well-established correlation between WM and Gf becomes non-significant when controlling for individual differences in AC, suggesting that AC mediates the relationship between WM and Gf.

text.text: These distinctions are important for understanding trust calibration.
WM may support monitoring by helping users keep recent automation successes and failures available.
Gf may support schema updating by helping users reason about whether changes in reliability reflect isolated failures or broader changes in automation performance.
AC may support trust calibration by regulating attention and helping users apply maintained information and reasoning to reliability-relevant cues.

Although existing automation and individual-differences research has primarily focused on WM (e.g., Rovira et al., 2017), the close relationship among WM, Gf, and AC suggests that these abilities may each contribute to automation schemas and, consequently, trust dynamics.

text.text: Examining all three abilities therefore allows us to test whether trust decline and recovery rely on the same cognitive mechanisms or on distinct components of cognition.

We make two assertions based on prior research; first that abilities affect schema quality (Gilbert & Rogers, 1999; Radvansky & Dijkstra, 2007; Valadao et al., 2015), and second that the schema quality will affect trust (Dzindolet et al., 2002; Merritt et al., 2015; Weis & Wiese, 2022).

text.text: From these assertions, this study has four hypotheses: • Hypothesis 1: Consistent with Rovira et al. (2017) when automation is reliable, individuals with lower WM will have higher trust than those with higher WM.

text.text: • Hypothesis 2: When automation becomes unreliable, individuals with lower WM will show less trust decline than those with higher WM.

Participants were informed they were collaborating with automation on a task, and that they should try to maximize their combined score.

text.text: Participants completed three experimental blocks with automated memory tasks and manual arithmetic tasks.
Automation reliability was manipulated across blocks and refers to the proportion of trials in which the automated aid produced the correct response.
The first and third blocks had 100% automation reliability, while the second block had 65% reliability (about 12 errors in about 33 trials).
Block 2 was therefore the failure block, whereas Blocks 1 and 3 represented perfectly reliable automation before and after the failure period.
Sixty-five percent reliability was chosen because it falls below the approximate 70% threshold at which imperfect automation may become more harmful than helpful.
Prior work suggests that below this level, human-automation performance can be worse than unaided performance, and trust tends to decline rapidly (Lee & See, 2004; Wickens & Dixon, 2007).

text.text: Thus, the 65% reliability block was intended to create a clearly unreliable automation period that would produce a measurable decline in trust while still allowing trust recovery to be examined once automation returned to 100% reliability.
Errors were either incorrect responses or offline status, equally distributed.
An automation status window provided real-time feedback, with color-coded responses indicating correctness.
Participants could only observe the memory subtask and automation activity without intervention, ensuring consistent exposure to reliability levels across participants.
This design was chosen to focus on trust in automation rather than reliance behaviors.
At the end of each block, participants were asked to evaluate their level of trust in the memory task aid using the question, "How much did you trust this automated memory aid?"
Responses were recorded on a visual analog scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 10 (extremely).
In this study, trust decline and trust recovery were operationalized using these self-reported trust ratings.
Trust decline refers to the change in trust ratings from Block 1, when the automation was 100% reliable, to Block 2, when reliability decreased to 65%.
Trust recovery refers to the change in trust ratings from Block 2 to Block 3, when automation reliability returned to 100%.

A singleitem trust measure was used based on findings by Patton and Wickens (2024), which demonstrated that it correlates more strongly with trusting behavior (e.g., dependence) compared to multi-item trust measures (e.g., Jian, Bisantz, and Drury, 2000).

From the 144 participants who provided complete data, we filtered participants according to the following behavioral rules that indicate inattentive responding.
Any participant who scored a zero on an ability test was removed (n = 10 dropped), as that indicated chance or non-engaged performance.

Participants with negative math scores on the secondary task were excluded, as negative scores indicated that they made little or no valid attempt to perform the concurrent arithmetic task.(n = 10 dropped).

Finally, participants whose trust ratings across all three blocks were identical were excluded (n = 13 dropped), as identical ratings across the 100%-65%-100% reliability manipulation suggested a lack of attention to the changing automation performance..

text.text: The pattern of correlations between WM, automation schema, and trust is consistent with this hypothesized mechanism linking abilities to trust.
We also included measures of AC and Gf, which are known to be associated with WM, for exploratory purposes.
To our surprise, these additional cognitive variables yielded unexpected findings.
No abilities predicted the decline of trust, and trust recovery was predicted by WM and Gf.
Finally, the extent to which trust fully recovered to pre-failure levels (trust change) was related to WM and AC.
Our general exploratory hypothesis that AC and Gf would play a role in trust dynamics was supported (hypothesis 4).
We expected to replicate prior research showing a negative relationship between WM and trust (Rovira et al., 2017), but our findings differed.

text.text: WM was not correlated with trust after exposure to 100% reliable automation (block 1).
However, WM and Gf were positively correlated to trust at the study's end, after experiencing varying reliability levels.
Two questions arise: Why wasn't WM correlated to trust after the first block?
And why might it be positively correlated, instead of negative as Rovira et al. demonstrated?
Methodological differences may explain these discrepancies.
Rovira et al. measured trust after exposure to 80% reliable automation, while our initial trust was measured after 100% reliable automation (block 1).
With no failures in the first block, there was no need to remember past failures to update an automation schema, thus no relationship with WM.
After experiencing different reliabilities, participants may have needed to remember and integrate/update their automation schema, requiring WM and Gf.
Moreover, our automation was only observable, while in Rovira et al., it assisted in the primary task.

text.text: Automation that actively assists necessarily draws more user attention to its behavior, potentially affecting the relationship between WM and trust.
The positive relationship between working memory (WM) and trust in our study, contrasting with Rovira et al.'s findings, may again be due to methodological differences.

text.text: When failures are this noticeable, users may respond with an immediate decline in trust that operates independently of higher-level cognitive resources.
This may explain why the decline in trust appeared relatively uniform across individuals who differed substantially in cognitive abilities.
Contrary to our hypothesis, we found WM and Gf were positively related to trust recovery.
This may be because individuals with higher WM can better remember recent automation performance while multitasking.
Those with higher Gf may more effectively integrate or update their automation schema with new performance information, guiding their trust ratings.
When errors cease, high Gf individuals may be better at updating their schema by discarding old information and incorporating new data.
In essence, WM may be crucial for monitoring automation performance, while Gf may be key for updating the automation schema.
The absence of a relationship between trust recovery and AC suggests that recovery doesn't require flexible deployment of WM and Gf, but rather relies on both abilities simultaneously.
Our results show that trust change from initial exposure to block 3 was related to WM and, to a lesser extent, AC.
Participants with higher WM demonstrated nearly full trust recovery (flat trust slope), while those with lower WM did not (negative trust slope).
This suggests that higher WM individuals may have more responsive trust calibration, with their trust ratings closely matching the actual reliability of the automation.
Lower WM individuals' trust at block 3 remained lower than at block 1, indicating less responsive calibration.
One factor that may contribute to this difference is relationship between WM and automation schema.
We found that all-or-none thinking was negatively related to WM.
Higher WM individuals were less likely to believe automations are completely useless after errors.
In contrast, lower WM individuals might have perceived the automation as broken after failures in block 2, leading to a permanent decrease in trust at block 3, even after errors were corrected.
Individuals with high AC lowered their trust at study's end, while low AC showed no change.
This counterintuitive finding may represent optimal trust calibration; high AC individuals likely incorporated the variable reliability (100%, ~65%, 100%) into their schema.
Consequently, their trust should be lower than after experiencing only 100% reliability (block 1).
Low AC individuals showed no trust changes between blocks 1 and 3, suggesting their ratings were based primarily on recent information.
They may have struggled to disengage from less relevant data (block 2's momentary reliability change, Gf-dependent) and to recall block 1 performance (WM-dependent) when forming an updated schema.
These results may illustrate the two types of trust calibration: short-term and long-term.

Short-term calibration (i.e., swift trust; Capiola et al., 2020; Meyerson et al., 1996) is trust from immediate experiences while long-term calibration (de Visser et al., 2020) incorporates both recent and historical performance.

text.text: WM might assist with moment-by-moment, short-term trust calibration, while AC may aid accurate long-term calibration by recalling past performance (WM) and updating the automation schema (Gf).
Our findings suggest that appropriate trust calibration depends on cognitive resources that vary across individuals.
This has direct implications for automation interface design, particularly for systems where trust recovery and long-term calibration are critical for safe and effective use.
Rather than designing interfaces that present performance information uniformly to all users, systems could benefit from adaptive or flexible displays that accommodate different cognitive profiles.
Our results point to three broad principles that may inform future interface design.
First, users with lower WM may benefit from explicit memory support through performance summaries and visual trend displays, reducing the cognitive burden of tracking automation behavior over time.

This is suggested by our finding that WM predicts trust recovery, which implies that high-WM individuals may be able to track recent performance internally while low-WM individuals may struggle to do so.

Second, AC influences how users weigh historical versus recent information, implying that interfaces should make both types of information available but may need to emphasize them differently for different users.

High-AC users benefit from comprehensive historical context that supports nuanced long-term calibration, while low-AC users may need recent performance emphasized to avoid over-weighting outdated information.

Third, given Gf's role in schema updating, explicit explanations of reliability changes can assist users (particularly those with lower Gf) in appropriately revising their understanding when system performance shifts.
There are several limitations that warrant more follow-up research.
First, participants could not intervene in the automated task, which may reduce their motivation to monitor automation performance and therefore influence trust.
To address this concern, we emphasized that participants' final score depended on both their own performance and the automation's performance.
This instruction encouraged participants to remain aware of the automation's reliability, and the observed trust changes across blocks confirm that they were indeed monitoring its performance.

Second, because the purpose of the research was to examine the relationship between abilities and trust change, we used a simplified task that was automated but was not tied to a specific domain or required specialized training.
While this may enhance generalizability of the results, it ignores task-specific factors that may influence trust such as risk, or domain (Pak et al., 2017).

Relatedly, the participants in our study were mostly college-aged students which reduced the generalizability to other populations.

Third, we hypothesized that any influence of cognitive abilities on trust was mediated by the automation schema that was dependent on various abilities (e.g., Radvansky & Dijkstra, 2007) which would then affect trust (e.g., Merritt et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Third, we hypothesized that any influence of cognitive abilities on trust was mediated by the automation schema that was dependent on various abilities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Radvansky & Dijkstra, 2007)</ref> which would then affect trust (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Merritt et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, we only measured the automation schema once and did not measure if it may have changed with exposure to automation.
In addition, we only measured one conception of the automation schema (perfect automation schema) which may only represent one kind of information contained in the user's knowledge structure.

Future research should explore more direct measurements of the schema (e.g., what information is contained in it), and assess it more frequently to definitely implicate the role of abilities in trust.

These results provide some insight into trust dynamics; namely that losing trust is easy (i.e., is independent of cognitive resources) but recovering trust is hard (i.e., it requires several abilities).

The notion that trust recovery is resource-constrained is consistent with recent theories of trust repair that suggest that the efficacy of active trust repair may be dependent on cognitive resources (Pak & Rovira, 2023).

text.text: The resource constraint may come from the need to update the knowledge structure (automation schema), which is likely effortful (i.e., requires cognitive resources; Chen, 2002).

text.text: It also gives an explanation for the age-related differences in trust recovery that have been previously observed (e.g., Sanchez et al., 2014).
text.formatted: It also gives an explanation for the age-related differences in trust recovery that have been previously observed (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Sanchez et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Age-related declines in a wide range of fluid abilities (McLaughlin & Pak, 2020) may make the trust recovery process slower or less responsive.
text.formatted: Age-related declines in a wide range of fluid abilities (McLaughlin & Pak, 2020) may make the trust recovery process slower or less responsive.

text.text: Effective trust calibration requires cognitive processes that vary across individuals, which highlights the need for automation designs that provide customizable and cognitively supportive features.
Such features can guide attention, support memory and reasoning, thereby helping users maintain appropriate trust, especially in multitasking or highworkload environments.
Current trust calibration interventions focusing on working memory (e.g., McGuirl & Sarter, 2006; Price et al., 2016) should be complemented with methods to enhance attention control and reasoning.
text.formatted: Current trust calibration interventions focusing on working memory (e.g., McGuirl & Sarter, 2006; Price et al., 2016) should be complemented with methods to enhance attention control and reasoning.

text.text: This could lead to more accurate automation schemas and better trust calibration.
For instance, ecological display design approaches (e.g., Skraaning & Jamieson, 2021) may reduce comprehension effort while improving automation schemas and trust calibration.
text.formatted: For instance, ecological display design approaches (e.g., Skraaning & Jamieson, 2021) may reduce comprehension effort while improving automation schemas and trust calibration.

text.text: Overall, this study extends trust in automation research by showing that passive trust recovery is shaped not only by automation reliability, but also by the cognitive abilities users bring to the interaction.
